vignette: Rafael Hernandez had been driving buses for over two decades, navigating the familiar streets of Los Angeles with ease. But on a fateful evening three years ago, his life took a drastic turn. He was stopped by police while driving home from work, allegedly for a minor traffic infraction. What ensued was a traumatic encounter that would leave an indelible mark on Rafael's psyche. The officers, Rafael recalled, were aggressive and dismissive of his concerns, eventually handcuffing him and detaining him for several hours without explanation. The memory of those handcuffs still haunted him - the feeling of being powerless, trapped, and disrespected by those sworn to protect him. When he finally managed to compose himself after the ordeal, Rafael couldn't shake off the sense that the world was no longer a safe place. Over time, Rafael began noticing changes in his behavior. He would suddenly become irritable, lashing out at passengers or colleagues for minor transgressions. His concentration started waning, and he found it increasingly difficult to focus on the road while driving. At home, Rafael developed an obsessive habit of checking that doors and windows were locked multiple times before feeling secure. The presence of police officers or even just their uniforms would send Rafael's mind racing back to that traumatic event. He began avoiding public gatherings, fearing encounters with law enforcement might trigger another panic attack. Conversations about the incident with friends or family members left him uneasy; talking about it made the memories feel too real. Rafael resorted to maladaptive coping strategies to manage his anxiety. When overwhelmed by thoughts of the traumatic event, he would instinctively cover his face with his hands, as if hiding from the world. Loud music or blaring TV became his go-to distractions at home, helping him mask the racing thoughts and memories that seemed to surface without warning. The loss of connection to his community weighed heavily on Rafael. He had always taken pride in being a responsible member of society, a good neighbor, and an active participant in local events. Now, however, he felt like a stranger in his own neighborhood, constantly on guard against potential threats. His mistrust extended beyond the police; people in general seemed untrustworthy to him now. One particularly distressing incident occurred when Rafael's bus broke down near a police station. As he waited for assistance, several officers approached him, asking routine questions about the vehicle's maintenance history. Rafael felt like he was reliving the traumatic event all over again - the same sense of powerlessness and vulnerability washed over him. This episode proved to be a turning point. Recognizing that his avoidance strategies were no longer sustainable, Rafael realized it was time to seek help. He couldn't continue living in fear, constantly questioning everyone's intentions, or perpetually feeling on edge. The thought of confronting these issues head-on terrified him, but he knew he had to try. Rafael's greatest fear now is that therapy will force him to relive the traumatic event without being able to shield himself from its impact. Yet, deep down, he hopes that by facing his fears and regaining control over his life, he might slowly begin rebuilding trust - not just in others but also in himself.
